analysis.one_liner: Lets states redirect federal health program money into their own universal health coverage plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees in November 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a state, or a group of states, apply to waive federal health insurance rules and set up its own universal health coverage program. The state would receive the federal money that would otherwise have been spent on its residents through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, TRICARE, and premium tax credits, and use it to run a public plan covering at least 95% of residents within five years. Coverage would have to be at least as comprehensive and affordable as what residents would have gotten under the federal programs, and every state program would be independently reviewed every five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of a state that adopts a plan — especially the uninsured, people with unaffordable deductibles, and people who lose coverage when they change jobs — would get comprehensive coverage through a publicly administered state program. People enrolled in Medicaid, CHIP, ACA marketplace plans, and federal employee or military coverage in those states would be folded into the state plan. American Indians and Alaska Natives who enroll would have all health insurance costs paid by the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state could pool the federal money it would otherwise receive for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, marketplace subsidies, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE into a single state-administered health plan [S2] [S3].
The state plan must cover all residents and be at least as comprehensive, affordable, and protective against high out-of-pocket costs as the federal programs it replaces [S3].
States must reach 95% coverage of residents within five years or face a 12-month grace period and possible termination of the waiver, and plans are independently reviewed every five years [S2] [S3].

Plans must be publicly administered, must include reproductive health care including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and states may contract with private entities only to administer the plan [S3].
The federal government would pay all health insurance costs for American Indians and Alaska Natives who enroll through a state program, honoring federal trust responsibilities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would keep spending roughly the same amount, passing it to states instead of through the replaced programs; states would bear any costs above the federal passthrough and must show a 10-year federal budget-neutral plan. Private health insurers in a participating state would lose much of the individual, small-group, and public-contract business that the state plan replaces, and employers would move out from under the employer mandate and ERISA rules in that state.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers; state budgets above federal funds

drawbacks.text: The waiver only passes federal money through to states; if a state's program costs more than the federal funds, the state must find the difference itself, and the bill requires the plan be budget-neutral for the federal government, meaning no new federal money [S3].

A waiver can be terminated if the state fails to reach 95% coverage within five years plus a 12-month grace period, so beneficiaries in a struggling state could face an abrupt transition back to federal programs [S3].

Moving Medicare, TRICARE, and federal employee beneficiaries into a state-run plan is a large administrative transition, and coverage rules would vary sharply at state borders, creating complexity for people and employers who cross state lines [S3].

Requiring every participating state plan to cover abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care would make the option unusable in states opposed to those mandates, limiting the bill to a small set of willing states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a state that chooses to participate, the bill offers a real path to universal coverage using money the state's residents already generate through federal programs, with guardrails requiring coverage at least as good as what people have now. The design is cautious — no new federal spending, five-year reviews, and termination for failure — but that same caution means the burden of making universal coverage work financially falls entirely on the participating state, and the mandate on reproductive coverage means only states already inclined toward universal coverage could use it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees when introduced, sat in the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and died when the Congress ended with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 7, 2023, by Rep. Ro Khanna along with 30 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3] [S4].

It was referred to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight, and Education and the Workforce — a referral pattern that gives each committee a veto over any piece of the bill [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on November 10, 2023, and again on December 17, 2024, but no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without any vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and other stakeholders in the existing federal and private insurance system are better off, since no state can use the waiver pathway to replace private and employer coverage with a public plan. The bill's supporters gained a floor vote nowhere; the option simply never existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the insurance status quo

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act of 2023 on November 7, 2023

for.name: 30 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it

against.name: House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Oversight, and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.role: Committees of referral under a Republican House majority
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill in over a year; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee from November 2023 until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 224 of 438 House seats and controlling committee schedules, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: In any state that adopts a plan, the public program would replace private individual-market, small-group, Medicaid managed care, and much employer-based coverage, eliminating those premium streams. The state may contract with private entities only to administer claims, not to sell the coverage the plan displaces.

In a participating state, employers would be freed from the employer-mandate penalty and from ERISA rules governing self-funded plans, potentially shifting health benefit costs onto the state program. That could benefit employers' budgets while removing coverage decisions from workplace control.

Providers would gain guaranteed coverage for nearly all patients and a single payer's simpler billing, but public plans typically pay less than private insurance. Indian health care providers would gain guaranteed payment at no less than in-network rates.
